newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian farmers shun presidential poll.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian farmers shun presidential poll.

text.p: Farmers preparing for winter in this small Bulgarian village dug their plots on Sunday, indifferent to a presidential election which they said would do little to improve their lot.
The 2,000 inhabitants of Negovan, 15 km (10 miles) northeast of the capital Sofia, used to breed pigs, sheep and cows for milk and meat but now say rising prices mean they cannot pay for fodder.
"Several months ago during the summer I had 120 cows but now there are 74," said village herdsman Assen Yordanov, 39.
He said many peasants had slaughtered their animals as the purchasing price for milk was too low and they could not cover their costs.

The polling station in the village school was deserted. Yordanov said he might vote later but did not expect things to improve immediately. "The chaos in the country is such that we cannot get better soon," he said.
Delays in implementing economic reform since the end of one-party communist rule in 1989 have brought Bulgaria to the edge of bankruptcy. Bread and power shortages loom during the approaching winter.

"Our life is so hard that it is frightening to live," said Olga Netkova, selling newspapers in the village square. "I do not think I will go to vote as I do not see how a president, whoever he is, can change things."

Villagers complained they could not cultivate all the land which was returned to them when communist-era cooperative farms were dismantled, as they could not pay private firms to hire machines for the sowing.
One group of women, who said they were still making up their minds on whether to vote, said their main concern was their children's future.
"My son is a soldier now and I cannot sleep for worrying whether he will find work after his army service," said Trayana Velichkova.

Opinion polls in the largely agricultural country of 8.4 million people show the opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov ahead of his main rival, Socialist culture minister Ivan Marazov but short of a majority in the first round.
If no candidate wins a majority, or if turnout is below 50 percent, there will be a second round next Sunday.
The indifference to the election was reflected in other rural areas.
In the southern ethnic Turkish village of Egrek, close to the Greek border, just 90 of the village's 760 registered electors had voted by early afternoon.
Thousands of ethnic Turks left Bulgaria in the 1980s when former Communist leader Todor Zhivkov forced them to adopt Bulgarian names and discouraged them from practising Islam.
Many Bulgarian ethnic Turks working in Turkey returned to vote in parliamentary elections in December 1994 but this time the turnout in the region appeared much lower.
Whole families preferred to take advantage of the sunny autumn weather to work in the fields.

"No one will come to sow our wheat for us and we don't want to die of starvation. The politicians are not coming here, they have forgotten us -- even God has forgotten us," said one member of a big Turkish family.
